text: You could sink Everest in this hole, with two kilometers to spare.
And after 150 years, we still can't say how deep it is.
Wait, I'm going in there?
This is the Challenger Deep, about 350 kilometers from Guam.
Rewind to 1875, sailors on HMS Challenger lowered a weighted rope.
It hit bottom at 8,184 meters. The deep still carries their ship's name.
Deepest spot on Earth. Probably.
Then came Sonar. 1951, 10,863 meters. 1957, a Soviet ship, 11,033.
That's half an Eiffel Tower of disagreement.
So why can't anyone agree?
Sonar doesn't measure depth.
It times an echo, then uses the speed of sound.
And in seawater, that speed changes with temperature, salt, and pressure.
Guess the speed wrong, and the bottom moves.
Don't look at me. I just bounce.
And the bottom isn't one point. It's three narrow basins.
So this year, a Japanese team mapped it again with five sound speed models.
Best answer, 10,927 meters. The models alone disagreed by 18. The twist? In 1984, a Japanese
ship got 10,920. 42 years later, the answer moved 7 meters. The deepest point on earth
isn't a number, it's a range. So how far down am I going? This is Boogal, follow for
more geography fun facts.
